Staphylococcal infections Staphylococci are Gram-positive bacteria pathogenic to man. Species may be differentiated by various methods, including the coagulase test. Those species of clinical im- portance are Staphylococcus aureus, which is usually co- agulase-positive, and Staph. epidermidis and Staph. sapro- phyticus, which are coagulase-negative. Staph. aureus colonises the skin and mucous membranes naturally and many people, including neonates, may be staphylococcal carriers from time to time. Localised Staph. aureus infections may follow surgery or trauma and com- monly result in abscess formation. Staphylococcal skin in- fections include impetigo and furunculosis. Conditions as- sociated with staphylococcal extracellular toxin production include staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, toxic shock syndrome, and staphylococcal food poisoning. Staphylococcal septicaemia is usually a consequence of local infection and may sometimes be associated with in- travascular or intraperitoneal catheters or with intravenous drug abuse. Septicaemia often results in staphylococcal endocarditis. Other possible complications of septicaemia are pneumonia and bone and joint infections, although in these cases aspiration or local trauma, respectively, may be the cause.
